key_risks.description: AI capacity may be misjudged. The filing warns that demand for cloud-based and AI products is evolving and difficult to forecast, and that overestimating demand or misaligning capacity may cause underutilization and impairment of balance sheet assets. The same investments are made at significant scale and on an accelerated timeline, in advance of fully developed revenue streams. FY2026 property and equipment, net, rose to $313.1 billion from $205.0 billion.

Margin dilution from AI infrastructure. Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell to 66% on continued AI infrastructure investment, and Intelligent Cloud cost of revenue rose 44% against 30% segment revenue growth. Total gross margin percentage compressed by roughly 80 to 90 basis points. Depreciation on newly built or leased capacity will flow into future cost of revenue regardless of demand.

Large lease and purchase commitments that are not yet commenced. Additional leases, primarily for datacenters, of $329.1 billion had not commenced at June 30, 2026, with some subject to contractual conditions, and will commence between fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2033 with terms of 1 to 20 years. Finance lease liabilities rose to $66.6 billion from $46.2 billion, and purchase commitments total roughly $194 billion, with about $169 billion due in fiscal 2027. These obligations are not in reported debt.

Counterparty concentration and related-party exposure to OpenAI. Microsoft holds an equity-method investment of approximately 25% on an as-converted basis, and OpenAI is a related party under ASC 850. Remaining performance obligation was $684 billion ($678 billion commercial), with only about 30% expected to be recognized within 12 months. Reported OpenAI gains boosted FY2026 EPS, and the filing does not break out OpenAI's share of the backlog.

Cash conversion after AI reinvestment. Operating cash flow rose $46.8 billion to $182.9 billion, but additions to property and equipment rose to roughly $115.9 billion. Dividends and buybacks (about $48.7 billion paid) consume a growing share of free cash flow, while cash and short-term investments fell to $76.8 billion from $94.6 billion.

Earnings quality and valuation of investments. Other income (expense), net, swung to $10.7 billion of income from an expense of $4.9 billion, driven by net recognized gains on investments and derivatives. Equity and other investments rose to $36.3 billion from $15.4 billion, including $24.6 billion of Level-less 'Other' equity investments valued at cost with adjustments, which are harder to value and can swing earnings.

Partners that are also competitors and significant customers of Azure could shift workloads. The filing flags that in some cases these parties are significant customers of Azure and other cloud services, which creates dependency and competitive risk in a capacity-constrained market.

bull_case: Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 41% in FY2026 with growth across all workloads, and Intelligent Cloud revenue rose 30% to $137.8 billion. The filing says demand exceeding available capacity limits the ability to serve customers, which points to demand rather than weakness.

Operating income grew 21% to $155.2 billion and operating margin expanded roughly 120 basis points to about 46.8%, even as gross margin percentage slipped. Opex growth of 7% against revenue growth of 18% is absorbing the AI cost drag.

Operating cash flow rose 34% to $182.9 billion, funding capex, a $3.64 per share dividend, and buybacks while total long-term debt (current and long-term portions) fell to about $40.3 billion from $43.2 billion.

Remaining performance obligation reached $684 billion ($678 billion commercial) with a weighted average duration of about 2.3 years, and about 30% (roughly $205 billion) is expected to be recognized within 12 months. This gives multi-year revenue visibility.
Adjusted diluted EPS excluding OpenAI items still grew about 22% to $17.28, so the core business is strong beyond mark-to-market gains.

Copilot (about 15 million paid seats, roughly 3.3% of the commercial base) and consumption-based pricing offer long-tail monetization optionality, and Azure efficiency gains could stabilize cloud gross margin near 66%.
Productivity and Business Processes grew 16% with operating income up 20%, giving a high-margin base of recurring Microsoft 365 revenue.
bear_case: Free cash flow fell about 6% to roughly $67.0 billion as capital additions rose about 80% to $115.9 billion. Roughly 110% of the incremental operating cash flow was reinvested, and dividends plus buybacks now absorb about 73% of free cash flow, up from about 59%.

Microsoft Cloud gross margin fell to 66%, Intelligent Cloud cost of revenue rose 44% against 30% revenue growth, and total gross margin percentage fell to about 68.0% from about 68.8%. Finance-lease property at cost rose about 53% to $82.7 billion, and finance lease cost rose about 65%, so depreciation could outrun revenue.

Datacenter leases not yet commenced total $329.1 billion, about five times recorded finance lease liabilities of $66.6 billion. Purchase commitments of about $194 billion, with about $169 billion due in fiscal 2027, mean the cash call is largely ahead.

Backlog quality is a concern: only about 30% of the $684 billion RPO converts within 12 months, and OpenAI (a roughly 25% equity-method related party, reported at about 45% of the backlog in an earlier quarter) concentrates counterparty risk.
GAAP EPS growth of 32% is flattered by OpenAI-related gains (about $0.67 per share) and by $10.7 billion of other income. Adjusted EPS growth was 22%.
Cash and short-term investments fell to $76.8 billion from $94.6 billion, while equity and other investments rose to $36.3 billion, a larger share of hard-to-value assets.
The filing itself warns of possible underutilization and asset impairment if AI demand is overestimated, and the stock has traded near a one-year low on AI spending concerns.

what_to_watch.text:
**Azure Growth Versus Cloud Gross Margin:** Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 41% in FY2026, Intelligent Cloud revenue grew 30%, and the filing notes demand exceeding available capacity, which supports growth continuing as new capacity lands. Bank of America expects Azure at or above the 39% to 40% guided range to be needed to support the stock. However, Microsoft Cloud gross margin fell to 66%, Intelligent Cloud cost of revenue rose 44% against 30% revenue growth, and segment operating income grew only 28%, so capacity constraint alone does not prove that incremental Azure revenue earns an adequate return.

-> Monitor Azure growth in constant currency against guidance, and whether Microsoft Cloud gross margin stabilizes near or above 66% rather than merely citing efficiency gains.

**Free Cash Flow and Capital Returns:** Operating cash flow rose 34% to $182.9 billion, but additions to property and equipment rose about 80% to roughly $115.9 billion, so free cash flow fell about 6% to roughly $67.0 billion. Dividends ($26.4 billion paid) and buybacks ($22.3 billion) now absorb about 73% of free cash flow versus about 59% a year earlier, and cash plus short-term investments fell to $76.8 billion from $94.6 billion. That said, operating cash flow growth is funding a front-loaded build-out, so a one-year dip may prove a trough if capacity converts into contracted backlog.

-> Monitor operating cash flow growth versus capex (management indicated more than $50 billion next quarter), the free cash flow payout ratio, and any change in buyback pace.

**Datacenter Leases and Off-Balance-Sheet Commitments:** The filing discloses $329.1 billion of leases, mostly for datacenters, that had not yet commenced, starting between fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2033, plus about $194 billion of purchase commitments with roughly $169 billion due in fiscal 2027. Finance lease liabilities already rose to $66.6 billion from $46.2 billion, and finance lease cost jumped about 65%. On the other hand, some arrangements are subject to contractual conditions, and one analyst expects part of the leases to be classified as operating, which would lower reported capex without changing the economic commitment.

-> Monitor finance versus operating lease classification, the amount of leases commencing in the next quarters, and capex reported with and without finance leases.

**Backlog Quality and OpenAI Concentration:** Remaining performance obligation reached $684 billion ($678 billion commercial, weighted average duration about 2.3 years), with about 30% expected to be recognized within 12 months, giving strong visibility. However, Microsoft owns roughly 25% of OpenAI on an as-converted basis, OpenAI is a related party, and news reports said OpenAI was about 45% of the commercial backlog in the December quarter. The filing does not break out that share at year-end, so the quality of the non-OpenAI portion is the key variable.

-> Monitor any updated disclosure of OpenAI's share of RPO, growth in non-OpenAI commitments, and related-party revenue and receivable balances.

**Earnings Quality and OpenAI Mark-to-Market Effects:** GAAP diluted EPS rose 32% to $17.95, but adjusted diluted EPS excluding OpenAI items rose about 22% to $17.28, and OpenAI-related gains added about $0.67 per share. Other income, net, swung to $10.7 billion from an expense of $4.9 billion. Even so, 22% growth ex-OpenAI is still strong, and operating income grew 21%, so the core business is not weak.

-> Monitor the gap between GAAP and adjusted EPS, other income (expense), net, and operating income growth as the cleaner read of momentum.

**Depreciation Wave and Gross Margin Trajectory:** Total gross margin percentage fell to about 68.0% from about 68.8%, cost of revenue grew 21% against revenue growth of 18%, and finance-lease property at cost rose from $53.9 billion to $82.7 billion. Operating margin still expanded about 120 basis points because operating expenses grew only 7%, which shows opex discipline is offsetting the drag. However, depreciation on the new asset base will keep landing in cost of revenue, so margin stability depends on utilization holding.

-> Monitor total and cloud gross margin percentage, the rate of operating expense growth, and any commentary on useful lives and depreciation growth.

**Copilot Monetization:** Microsoft disclosed about 15 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, roughly 3.3% of a commercial base of about 450 million, which has been cited as a shortfall. Conversely, low penetration is also optionality, and analysts see upside from consumption-based Copilot pricing and OpenAI economics. The filing notes higher Copilot advertising expenses in Productivity and Business Processes, where operating income grew 20%.

-> Monitor updated paid-seat counts, Productivity and Business Processes growth versus 16%, and any disclosure of Copilot revenue contribution.
